main_claims: The proposed DynoNet model effectively integrates semantically rich utterances with structured knowledge to represent open-ended dialogue states.
DynoNet is more effective at achieving the common goal in symmetric collaborative dialogues compared to baseline neural and rule-based models.

The new symmetric collaborative dialogue setting and the collected 11K human-human dialogue corpus push the boundaries of existing dialogue systems and exhibit diverse linguistic and strategic elements.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents a logically structured argument, moving from identifying a gap in existing dialogue systems (between task-oriented and open-domain) to proposing a novel symmetric collaborative dialogue setting and a corresponding large-scale human-human dataset. It then introduces DynoNet, a neural model designed to address the challenges of this setting by integrating structured knowledge with open-ended utterances via dynamic knowledge graph embeddings. The paper systematically evaluates DynoNet against baselines using both automatic and human metrics, including ablation studies to validate core architectural choices. A notable strength is the explicit discussion of discrepancies in human evaluation, which adds a layer of critical self-awareness. While the overall flow is coherent, certain methodological assumptions and the characterization of baselines could introduce subtle biases that affect the strength of some claims.
logical_argument_graph: P1: Existing dialogue systems (task-oriented, open-domain) are insufficient for handling rich, open-ended dialogue states while interfacing with structured knowledge (C1).
P2: A new 'symmetric collaborative dialogue' setting is proposed, requiring agents to identify a shared item from private KBs through open-ended communication.
P3: A large (11K) human-human dialogue corpus is collected for this setting, demonstrating diverse linguistic and strategic elements that necessitate powerful representation (C4).
P4: DynoNet, a neural model with dynamic knowledge graph embeddings, is proposed to integrate semantically rich utterances with structured knowledge to represent open-ended dialogue states (C2).
P5: DynoNet's architecture includes a dynamic knowledge graph, graph embedding with node features, mention vectors, recursive message passing, and entity abstraction (C5).
P6: Humans exhibit strategic behavior in this task, such as prioritizing attributes with fewer unique values and focusing on frequent entities (C7).

P7: DynoNet is evaluated against baselines (StanoNet, Rule) using automatic metrics (cross-entropy, language variation, discourse behavior, task effectiveness, strategic behavior) and human evaluations (partner, third-party).
P8: DynoNet achieves lower test loss, more human-like discourse, higher task effectiveness, and better partner satisfaction than baselines (C3).
P9: DynoNet successfully matches human strategic behavior, unlike the Rule baseline (C8).
P10: Ablation studies confirm that dynamic knowledge graph embeddings, message passing, and entity abstraction are crucial for DynoNet's performance (C5).
P11: A discrepancy is observed between partner and third-party human evaluation modes regarding fluency and human-likeness, suggesting different interpretive criteria (C6).

C: DynoNet effectively addresses the challenges of symmetric collaborative dialogue by integrating structured knowledge and open-ended language, demonstrating superior performance and human-likeness, supported by a novel dataset and architectural components, while also highlighting complexities in human evaluation.

concerns.title: Bias from Training Only on Successful Dialogues
concerns.description: The decision to train models exclusively on successful dialogues (Assumption A4) could introduce a bias. While this might optimize for ideal task completion, it may prevent the model from learning how to handle or recover from common conversational errors, misunderstandings, or less optimal paths, potentially limiting its robustness in real-world, imperfect interactions. This impacts the generalizability of the 'effectiveness' claim (C3).
evidence: We randomly split the data into train, dev, and test sets and only train on successful dialogues.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Discuss the potential limitations of training solely on successful dialogues and consider exploring strategies for incorporating unsuccessful dialogue data or error recovery mechanisms in future work. Acknowledge this as a scope limitation.

concerns.title: Unclear Robustness of Rule-Based Baseline
concerns.description: The paper claims the 'Rule' baseline is 'strong' (Assumption A7), but its description as having a 'pattern-matching semantic parser, a rule-based policy, and a templated generator' suggests a potentially less flexible or robust system compared to more advanced rule-based or hybrid approaches. If the baseline is not truly representative of a strong rule-based system, the performance gains of DynoNet over 'Rule' might be overstated, weakening the comparative claims (C3, C8).
evidence: We compare DynoNet with its static cousion (StanoNet) and a strong rule-based system (Rule).

Rule maintains weights for each entity and each item in the KB to decide what to talk about and which item to select. It has a pattern-matching semantic parser, a rule-based policy, and a templated generator. See Appendix G for details.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide more detailed justification or evidence for the 'strength' of the Rule baseline, perhaps by comparing its design to other state-of-the-art rule-based systems in similar domains, or by discussing its limitations more explicitly.

concerns.title: Reliance on Undetailed Rule-Based Entity Linking
concerns.description: The model relies on a 'rule-based lexicon to link text spans to entities' (Assumption A3), with details relegated to an appendix. Entity linking is a critical upstream component; any inaccuracies or limitations in this lexicon could propagate errors throughout the dynamic knowledge graph and impact the model's understanding and generation, thereby weakening the empirical evidence for DynoNet's effectiveness (C2, C3). The lack of detail or evaluation of this component's robustness is a structural weakness.
evidence: We use a rule-based lexicon to link text spans to entities. See details in Appendix D.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide more details on the rule-based lexicon's coverage, accuracy, and any error analysis in the main text or a more prominent appendix section. Discuss how potential errors in entity linking might affect DynoNet's performance.

comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar in principle: This work emphasizes that 'one vector is not enough' and argues for entity-augmented distributed semantics, moving towards combining distributed and formal semantics. This aligns with DynoNet's approach of using dynamic knowledge graph embeddings to enrich utterance representations with structured knowledge, going beyond simple vector representations.

Similar in problem space: This work discusses challenges in building highly interactive dialogue systems, particularly the difficulty of learning interactive behaviors and porting systems to new domains. The current paper's introduction of a new symmetric collaborative setting and a model designed for open-ended interaction directly addresses these challenges by attempting to bridge the gap between structured and unstructured dialogue.

Contextual relevance: This document describes the Dialog State Tracking Challenge (DSTC) series, which is highly relevant to task-oriented dialogue systems and the challenge of maintaining dialogue state. DynoNet's dynamic knowledge graph can be seen as an advanced approach to dialogue state representation, aiming to overcome limitations of traditional slot-filling or fixed-state tracking in more open-ended contexts.

General relevance to neural networks in NLP, specifically mentioning work on Deep Neural Network Approach for the Dialog State Tracking Challenge (Henderson et al., 2013). This provides a broader context for neural approaches to dialogue state modeling, which DynoNet builds upon by introducing dynamic knowledge graph embeddings.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The paper's introduction of a novel symmetric collaborative dialogue setting, coupled with a large-scale human-human corpus and a model architecture (DynoNet) specifically designed to handle dynamic knowledge graph embeddings for open-ended dialogue, represents a distinct contribution. While the core components (KGs, dynamic embeddings, message passing) exist, their integration and application to this specific, complex dialogue setting appear novel. The methodological concerns raised are distinct from the inherent novelty of the proposed framework.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If the 'Rule' baseline were demonstrably state-of-the-art for rule-based systems in similar complex dialogue tasks, DynoNet's performance gains would be even more impactful.

If the model could demonstrate robust error recovery or adaptation when trained on a mix of successful and unsuccessful dialogues, its real-world applicability and perceived human-likeness would significantly increase.

If the entity linking component were shown to be highly accurate and robust across diverse linguistic expressions, it would further solidify the foundation of the dynamic knowledge graph and DynoNet's overall performance.
If the paper offered a framework or guidelines for reconciling the discrepancies in human evaluation, it would provide a valuable methodological contribution to the field.

prior_stage_inputs: The paper introduces a novel symmetric collaborative dialogue setting and a large-scale human-human dialogue corpus (11K dialogues).
It proposes DynoNet, a neural model with dynamic knowledge graph embeddings, designed to integrate semantically rich utterances with structured knowledge for open-ended dialogue states.
The paper claims DynoNet outperforms baseline neural and rule-based models in task effectiveness and human-likeness, supported by automatic and human evaluations.
Key components of DynoNet, such as dynamic knowledge graph embeddings, message passing, and entity abstraction, are highlighted as crucial for its performance.
The paper also contributes to evaluation methodology by comparing partner and third-party human evaluation modes, noting discrepancies in how 'fluency' and 'human-likeness' are perceived.
A strategic aspect of human behavior in the dataset, focusing on attributes with fewer unique values and frequent entities, is identified and shown to be matched by DynoNet.
specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This audit focuses on the methodological soundness, reproducibility, and robustness of the proposed DynoNet model, the new dialogue setting, and its evaluation. The paper introduces a novel symmetric collaborative dialogue setting and a substantial human-human dataset, which are significant contributions. The DynoNet model's core idea of dynamic knowledge graph embeddings with message passing and entity abstraction is well-motivated and supported by ablation studies. The evaluation setup is comprehensive, employing both automatic metrics and a dual human evaluation approach (partner and third-party), with a valuable discussion on their discrepancies. However, several methodological assumptions, particularly regarding the training data selection (only successful dialogues) and the detailed specification of the rule-based baseline and entity linking lexicon, introduce concerns about the generalizability and full validity of the comparative claims. The observed instance of the model 'lying' also flags a robustness issue regarding factual grounding. Overall, the methodology is largely sound, but specific areas require greater transparency and consideration of broader applicability.
logical_argument_graph: P1: Current dialogue systems struggle with open-ended states and integrating structured knowledge (Section 1).
P2: A symmetric collaborative dialogue setting, where agents share a goal but have private KBs, encourages open-ended dialogue acts while requiring structured knowledge (Section 1, C1).
P3: A large-scale human-human corpus (11K dialogues) was collected for this setting, exhibiting diverse linguistic and strategic elements (Section 2.2, C4).
P4: The DynoNet model is proposed to address P1 and P2 by modeling dialogue state as a dynamic knowledge graph with evolving node embeddings (Section 3, C2).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper introduces a novel symmetric collaborative dialogue setting designed to bridge the gap between traditional task-oriented and open-domain chat systems, arguing that existing approaches struggle with the open-ended dialogue states and rich semantics inherent in such tasks. To address this, the authors propose DynoNet, a neural model that integrates semantically rich utterances with structured knowledge by modeling the dialogue state as a dynamic knowledge graph with evolving node embeddings. This model incorporates novel designs like entity abstraction and message passing to propagate contextual information across the graph. A significant contribution is a large-scale (11K human-human dialogues) corpus collected for this setting, which is shown to exhibit diverse linguistic and strategic elements. Through comprehensive automatic and human evaluations (including a comparison of partner and third-party evaluation methodologies), the authors demonstrate that DynoNet is more effective, generates more human-like dialogues, and better captures human strategic behavior compared to baseline neural and rule-based models. The core reasoning is that by dynamically updating and propagating context within a structured knowledge graph, DynoNet can maintain a richer, more flexible dialogue state representation than static or unstructured memory approaches, thereby improving performance in complex collaborative tasks.
logical_argument_graph: Existing task-oriented dialogue systems are limited by rigid pre-defined states and fixed acts, while open-domain systems lack structured knowledge integration for goal-oriented tasks (C1).
A symmetric collaborative dialogue setting, which is task-oriented but encourages open-ended acts, is proposed to bridge this gap, requiring more powerful representation (C1, C4).
A large-scale human-human corpus (11K dialogues) is collected for this new setting, exhibiting diverse linguistic and strategic elements (C4).

DynoNet, a neural model, is proposed to effectively integrate semantically rich utterances with structured knowledge by representing the dialogue state as a dynamic knowledge graph with evolving node embeddings (C2).

Dynamic knowledge graph embeddings, message passing between nodes, and entity abstraction are crucial components for DynoNet's performance, providing contextually-defined, structural node embeddings (C5).
DynoNet is more effective at achieving the common goal in symmetric collaborative dialogues compared to baseline neural and rule-based models, as shown by automatic and human evaluations (C3).
DynoNet generates more human-like dialogues and achieves higher partner satisfaction, particularly in cooperation, compared to baselines (C3).
DynoNet successfully matches human strategic behavior, such as favoring attributes with fewer unique values and more frequent entities to reduce search space (C7, C8).
Analysis of human evaluation methodologies reveals a discrepancy between partner and third-party evaluation modes, with different criteria influencing ratings for fluency and human-likeness (C6).
The new setting, dataset, and DynoNet provide unique opportunities for studying pragmatics and human strategies in dialogue, serving as a stepping stone towards more complex dialogues.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript introduces a novel conceptual framework for dialogue systems by defining a 'symmetric collaborative dialogue setting' that explicitly bridges the gap between traditional task-oriented systems (with predefined states and acts) and open-domain chat systems (lacking structured knowledge). This setting, where two agents with private knowledge must collaboratively identify a shared item through open-ended communication, represents a significant departure from prevalent dialogue paradigms. To address the challenges of this new setting, the paper proposes DynoNet, a neural model that dynamically represents dialogue state as an evolving knowledge graph. The disruptive novelty lies in DynoNet's integration of semantically rich, unstructured utterances with structured knowledge through dynamic knowledge graph embeddings, message passing between structured entities, and an 'entity abstraction' mechanism. This approach moves beyond static representations or purely RNN-based state tracking, offering a new way to model complex, context-dependent dialogue states that are crucial for the proposed collaborative setting. The accompanying large-scale human-human corpus further supports this new conceptualization by providing rich data that exhibits diverse linguistic and strategic phenomena, which existing systems struggle to capture.

comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: This work explores entity-augmented distributed semantics for discourse relations, arguing that a single vector is insufficient and that entity chains tie discourse together. This aligns with DynoNet's core idea of integrating structured entities (via KG) with distributed representations (embeddings) and dynamically propagating information, moving beyond purely vectorial representations to capture richer discourse context. Both works acknowledge the limitations of purely distributional semantics for complex linguistic phenomena.

This paper highlights challenges in building highly interactive dialogue systems, noting that learning interactive behaviors differs fundamentally from input-output mappings and requires new approaches that make fewer assumptions and can model human cognitive processing. It also discusses the difficulty of porting systems to new domains due to tied-to-specific-decision-points 'nodules of interactivity'. DynoNet's dynamic KG and open-ended nature directly address the need for more flexible, learned representations and less reliance on hand-crafted intermediate states, aligning with the call for new methods for interactive behaviors.

The paper explicitly states similarity to EntNet in that node/entity embeddings are updated recurrently given new utterances. However, it differentiates itself by structuring entities as a knowledge graph and propagating context on the graph. This highlights that while recurrent memory updates are a shared concept, DynoNet's *structured propagation* of information between entities in a KG is a key distinction and a source of its novelty.

uncertainty_flags: The paper acknowledges a discrepancy between partner and third-party human evaluations, suggesting that 'human-likeness' and 'fluency' can be perceived differently depending on the evaluator's role (participant vs. observer) and criteria (coherence/task success vs. informality/intuition). This introduces uncertainty in how 'human-likeness' should be definitively measured or interpreted.

The paper notes that DynoNet 'lied' in one example (Table 6), indicating a potential issue with factual correctness or grounding despite overall good performance. This raises uncertainty about the model's robustness in maintaining truthfulness.
alternative_interpretations: One could interpret the 'symmetric collaborative dialogue' setting as an incremental extension of multi-party task-oriented dialogue systems, rather than a fundamentally new paradigm. However, the emphasis on *open-ended dialogue acts* and the explicit bridging of task-oriented and open-domain systems suggests a more significant conceptual shift.

The 'dynamic knowledge graph embeddings' could be seen as an application of existing graph neural network (GNN) principles to dialogue state tracking, rather than a disruptive innovation in GNNs themselves. However, its application to dynamically evolving dialogue states, combined with entity abstraction, in a setting designed to challenge traditional state representations, positions it as disruptive within the dialogue systems domain.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper introduces a novel symmetric collaborative dialogue setting and a large-scale human-human corpus, which are well-supported contributions. The core claims regarding the DynoNet model's architecture, its integration of structured knowledge with open-ended utterances via dynamic knowledge graph embeddings, and the crucial role of its components (message passing, entity abstraction) are strongly supported by the model description and ablation studies. Claims about DynoNet's superior performance in effectiveness and human-likeness compared to baselines are largely supported by automatic and human evaluations, though nuanced by the paper's own acknowledgment of a 'lying' instance and prior reviewer concerns about the transparency and strength of the rule-based baseline. The analysis of human strategic behavior and DynoNet's ability to match it is also well-evidenced. The paper's observation and analysis of discrepancies between partner and third-party human evaluation methodologies are robustly presented. However, the generalizability of effectiveness claims is partially limited by the methodological choice to train exclusively on successful dialogues, and the foundational accuracy of the rule-based entity linking lexicon remains an underlying assumption impacting the entire system's grounding.

Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: cs committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct. There is already a policy on review incentives and sanctions, including temporary bans on (re-)submission or commitment to ACL venues. To add to the above points, the reviews that look like they were written by ChatGPT overall decrease the faith in the peer review process. According to this study, there is more generated text in ‘reviews which report lower confidence, were submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to respond to author rebuttals’. All these factors generally correspond to the type of unmotivated reviewer that, as authors, we would prefer to avoid. The increased ratio of such reviews also attunes the community to reviews that sound like they were generated. Generally, reviews are valued for their content rather than language, so your thoughts are more likely to be appreciated if they come in your voice (even if with linguistic imperfections). Finally: some authors actually count on you to use generative AI, and include hidden prompt injections intended to manipulate your assistant into giving a positive review! If you notice anything like that, please raise it with the chairs, such submissions should be desk rejected. What about the authors, can they use generative AI? The ACL policy on publication ethics discusses various cases with different degrees of acceptability.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.
